t.1.9.1: The Sūta said: While those brahmins were seated there all around, Ruru, deeply grief-stricken, went into the dense forest and cried aloud.
t.1.9.2: Then he, struck down by grief, lamenting much and piteously, spoke these words in his sorrow, thinking of his beloved Pramadvarā.
t.1.9.3: That slender-limbed one lies upon the ground, deepening the sorrow of me and of all her kinsmen. What grief could be greater than this?
t.1.9.4: If I have given gifts, if I have practiced austerities, or if I have duly honored my teachers, then by that merit let my beloved come back to life.
t.1.9.5: As surely as I have, from my very birth, kept my self restrained and held firm to my vows, so may the lovely Pramadvarā rise up this very day!
t.1.9.6: What you say in words out of grief, O Ruru, is in vain; for, O righteous one, there is no life left for a mortal whose lifespan is spent.
t.1.9.8: And a means for this was ordained long ago by the great-souled gods; if you are willing to carry it out, you will win back this Pramadvarā.
t.1.9.7: This pitiable daughter of a gandharva and an apsaras has reached the end of her life; therefore, dear son, do not in any way give your mind over to grief.
t.1.9.9: Ruru said: What means has been devised by the gods? Tell me truly, O sky-ranger. Having heard it, I shall do it accordingly; you should save me.
t.1.9.10: Give half of your life to the maiden, O delight of the Bhṛgus; in this way, O Ruru, your wife Pramadvarā will rise up.
t.1.9.11: Ruru said: I give half of my life to the maiden, O best of sky-rovers; let my beloved arise, adorned with beauty, grace and ornaments.
t.1.9.12: Then the king of the Gandharvas and the messenger of the gods, those two most excellent ones, approached Dharmarāja and spoke these words to him.
t.1.9.14: O messenger of the gods, if you so wish, let Pramadvarā, the wife of Ruru, rise up, endowed with half of Ruru's own lifespan.
t.1.9.13: O Dharmarāja, by half of Ruru's life, let Ruru's wife, the lovely Pramadvarā, rise up, dead though she is, if you so deem fit.
t.1.9.15: When this had been said, the maiden Pramadvarā, the fair-complexioned one, then rose up as if from sleep, by means of half of that Ruru's lifespan.
t.1.9.16: For this has indeed been seen, and so shall I bring it to pass: 'Of the greatly extended lifespan of Ruru of supreme splendour, let half diminish for the sake of his wife.'
t.1.9.18: Having obtained a wife hard to win, radiant as the filaments of a lotus, he, firm in his vows, made a vow for the destruction of the crooked-moving serpents.
t.1.9.17: Then, on a chosen day, their fathers joyfully performed their marriage, and the two of them took delight in each other, each seeking the other's welfare.
t.1.9.19: Seeing any snakes, he, filled with fierce wrath, always seizes a weapon and strikes down whichever of them come near.
t.1.9.20: Once the brahmin Ruru went to a great forest, and there he saw a ḍuṇḍubha snake lying, advanced in years.
t.1.9.21: Then the enraged brahmin, raising his staff, which was like the staff of Death, struck him; and then the ḍuṇḍubha spoke to him.
t.1.9.22: I have done you no wrong at all today, O ascetic rich in austerities. Why then, in your fury, filled with rage, do you strike me?
